paper.title: TBATS in smooth: its formulation, and its accuracy against forecast::tbats and AutoTBATS on hourly data

declarations.competing_interests: The guarantor is the author and maintainer of the smooth package whose TBATS the study evaluates.

paper.summary: TBATS forecasts series with several seasonal cycles, such as hourly electricity use with daily and weekly patterns. The smooth package for R and Python builds TBATS inside its general state space framework. Simulated checks show that, without ARMA terms, it is the same model as the original TBATS of De Livera, Hyndman and Snyder to rounding error; its ARMA terms differ, adding a separate component instead of modelling the errors. On the 414 hourly series of the M4 competition, forecasting 48 hours ahead, smooth's TBATS ranked as more accurate than the TBATS of R's forecast package and of Python's statsforecast, and took about 58% of the forecast package's time. On one week of 370 hourly electricity series, it was more accurate than repeating the last week, but not shown to differ from the other two. Assuming normally distributed errors made it faster, with intervals that covered fewer values than intended.
paper.correction_reason: The paper had no summary and did not state why the ARMA part of smooth's TBATS differs from De Livera's in effect: a summary in plain language is added; a formal claim (C21, with its condition C22 and proof E6) shows that ARMA errors pass the ARMA's persistence into the level, while ADAM's additive ARMA component leaves the level a fixed share of each shock; the highlights are amended; and the equation of the harmonic states in D1 is set on a line of its own.

definitions.definition:
TBATS of the smooth package (R `tbats()`, Python `TBATS`): a linear single-source-of-error state space model of the Box-Cox transform $y_t^{(\lambda)}$ of the series, built on ADAM's state space core,
$$\begin{aligned} y_t^{(\lambda)} &= w^\top v_{t-\boldsymbol{l}} + \epsilon_t, \\ v_t &= F v_{t-\boldsymbol{l}} + g \epsilon_t, \end{aligned}$$
where $v_{t-\boldsymbol{l}}$ takes each state at its own lag. The level $l_t$ and the trend $b_t$ are those of ETS(A,N,N), ETS(A,A,N) or ETS(A,Ad,N),
$$\begin{aligned} l_t &= l_{t-1} + \phi b_{t-1} + \alpha \epsilon_t, \\ b_t &= \phi b_{t-1} + \beta \epsilon_t. \end{aligned}$$
Each harmonic $j = 1, \dots, k_i$ of each period $m_i$, with frequency $\lambda_{ij} = 2 \pi j / m_i$, is two states $v^{(ij)}_1$ and $v^{(ij)}_2$ with lags 1 and 2 in the ARIMA slot of ADAM's core,
$$\begin{aligned} u_{ij,t} &= v^{(ij)}_{1,t-1} + v^{(ij)}_{2,t-2}, \\ v^{(ij)}_{1,t} &= 2 \cos(\lambda_{ij}) \, u_{ij,t} + \gamma_{1i} \epsilon_t, \\ v^{(ij)}_{2,t} &= -u_{ij,t} + \left(\sin(\lambda_{ij}) \gamma_{2i} - \cos(\lambda_{ij}) \gamma_{1i}\right) \epsilon_t, \end{aligned}$$
so that, with the backshift operator $B$,
$$(1 - 2 \cos(\lambda_{ij}) B + B^2) \, u_{ij,t} = \left(\gamma_{1i} B + (\sin(\lambda_{ij}) \gamma_{2i} - \cos(\lambda_{ij}) \gamma_{1i}) B^2\right) \epsilon_t.$$
The measurement equation is
$$y_t^{(\lambda)} = l_{t-1} + \phi b_{t-1} + \sum_i \sum_{j=1}^{k_i} u_{ij,t} + a_t + \epsilon_t,$$
where $a_t$ is an optional ARMA component of ADAM: an additive block of states whose output enters the measurement equation, not ARMA errors. $\lambda \in [0, 1]$ is estimated by likelihood with the Jacobian of the transform. The harmonics are preselected by information criterion on a global regression of the transformed series on Fourier terms, and the trend and the ARMA orders are selected by AICc. With the default `distribution="auto"`, the structure is selected with the generalised normal distribution of $\epsilon_t$, and the closest of the normal, Laplace and S distributions to its estimated shape is then fitted on that structure. Code: R/adam-tbats.R and python/src/smooth/adam_general/core/tbats/ of the smooth repository, at the code versions the evidence names.

TBATS of De Livera, Hyndman and Snyder (2011): for the Box-Cox transform $y_t^{(\lambda)}$,
$$\begin{aligned} y_t^{(\lambda)} &= l_{t-1} + \phi b_{t-1} + \sum_i \sum_{j=1}^{k_i} s^{(i)}_{j,t-1} + d_t, \\ l_t &= l_{t-1} + \phi b_{t-1} + \alpha d_t, \\ b_t &= \phi b_{t-1} + \beta d_t, \\ s^{(i)}_{j,t} &= \cos(\lambda_{ij}) s^{(i)}_{j,t-1} + \sin(\lambda_{ij}) s^{*(i)}_{j,t-1} + \gamma_{1i} d_t, \\ s^{*(i)}_{j,t} &= -\sin(\lambda_{ij}) s^{(i)}_{j,t-1} + \cos(\lambda_{ij}) s^{*(i)}_{j,t-1} + \gamma_{2i} d_t, \\ d_t &= \sum_{k=1}^{p} \varphi_k d_{t-k} + \sum_{k=1}^{q} \theta_k \epsilon_{t-k} + \epsilon_t, \end{aligned}$$
with $\lambda_{ij} = 2 \pi j / m_i$: ARMA(p, q) errors $d_t$ drive every state.

The tbats() function of the R package forecast (Hyndman et al.), De Livera et al.'s TBATS with its own model selection, called with seasonal.periods = c(24, 168), single-threaded, otherwise default settings.
AutoTBATS of the Python package statsforecast (Nixtla), called with season_length = [24, 168], otherwise default settings.
ADAM ETS of smooth's Python port, ADAM(model='ZXZ', lags=[24, 168]) with its default settings: ETS with a daily and a weekly seasonal component selected by AICc.
Seasonal naive forecast repeating the last 168 observations (the last week) of the training sample.

The 414 hourly series of the M4 competition (Makridakis et al., 2020), training samples of 700 or 960 observations and test samples of 48, from the Mcompetitions/M4-methods repository (Dataset/Train/Hourly-train.csv, Dataset/Test/Hourly-test.csv).
The M4 hourly training samples with their last 48 observations held out as a validation test: fitting on observations 1..n-48 and evaluating on n-47..n; never the official test samples.
Each method is fitted once to each training sample and forecasts h = 1..48 steps ahead from its end; no refits, no rolling origin.

Mean absolute scaled error of a series over the horizon $h = 48$,
$$\mathrm{MASE} = \frac{\frac{1}{h} \sum_{j=1}^{h} |y_{n+j} - \hat y_{n+j}|}{\frac{1}{n-24} \sum_{t=25}^{n} |y_t - y_{t-24}|},$$
scaled by the in-sample mean absolute seasonal difference at lag 24, as in M4.

Geometric mean over series of the ratio of the [[D10:MASE]] of method A to that of method B; below 1, A is more accurate. Its 99% confidence interval is the exponential of the t-interval of the mean log ratio over series.
Share of the test values of a set of series and horizons that lie inside the 95% prediction intervals of a method.
Wall-clock seconds to fit a method to one training sample and produce its forecasts and intervals, single-threaded.

Deterministic checks of smooth TBATS against its specification, per seed: (H1) random parameters, initial states and series of 300 observations simulated by De Livera's recursion with normal errors, for the periods {24}, {7.3}, {24, 168}, {7.3, 30.4}, no/additive/damped trend and lambda in {1, 0.5, 0}, fitted by smooth TBATS with all parameters and initial states fixed; (H2) a noise-free series of 300 observations made of a random level and random harmonics of the periods 7.3 and 24, fitted with random fixed persistence and initial='backcasting'; (H3) nine random pairs of alpha in (0.05, 0.95) and |phi| in (0.05, 0.95) for a local level with AR(1), the impulse response w'F^(j-1)g at j = 1..20 read from the fitted model's matrices. Code: claimset-code/smooth-tbats/formulation_checks.py.

The Nemenyi test as computed by greybox's rmcb (distribution 'tukey', ties averaged): the methods are ranked within each series by the error measure, and two methods differ at level $1 - \alpha$ when their mean ranks over series differ by more than the critical distance
$$\mathrm{CD} = \frac{q_{1-\alpha}(k, \infty)}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{\frac{k (k + 1)}{6 N}}$$
for $k$ methods and $N$ series.

Root mean squared scaled error of a series over the horizon $h = 48$,
$$\mathrm{RMSSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{h} \sum_{j=1}^{h} (y_{n+j} - \hat y_{n+j})^2}{\frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{t=2}^{n} (y_t - y_{t-1})^2}},$$
scaled by the in-sample root mean squared first difference of the fitting sample, as in M5.

Geometric mean over series of the ratio of the [[D16:RMSSE]] of method A to that of method B; below 1, A is more accurate. Its 99% confidence interval is the exponential of the t-interval of the mean log ratio over series.

The 370 hourly series of electricity consumption (kW) of clients of a Portuguese utility in GluonTS's electricity_nips archive (SR3), drawn from UCI ElectricityLoadDiagrams20112014: each series is the archive's training series extended by its last test window, ending 2014-09-08 01:00, 1249 to 6001 hours long.

Seven daily forecast origins over the last week of each series: the last one 48 hours before its end, the others 24, 48, ..., 144 hours earlier. At each origin each method is fitted to the 1008 preceding hours (six weeks) and forecasts 48 hours ahead; the RMSSE and the interval coverage of a series are averaged over its seven origins.

[[D1:smooth TBATS]] with the normal distribution of $\epsilon_t$: `TBATS(lags=[1, 24, 168], distribution="dnorm")` of the Python smooth package, every other setting at its default. The structure is selected and fitted with the normal distribution only, instead of the generalised normal distribution followed by the closest named distribution of the default `distribution="auto"`.

evidence.foundation: linear difference equations and power series in the backshift operator $B$

steps.statement: Under ARMA errors, $\phi(B) d_t = \theta(B) \epsilon_t$ with $\phi(B)$ stationary gives $d_t = \psi(B) \epsilon_t = \sum_{k \ge 0} \psi_k \epsilon_{t-k}$, with $\psi(B) = \theta(B) / \phi(B)$, $\psi_0 = 1$, $\psi_k \to 0$ and $\sum_{k \ge 0} \psi_k = \psi(1) = \theta(1) / \phi(1)$.

The level of the ARMA-errors model moves by $l_t - l_{t-1} = \alpha d_t = \alpha \psi(B) \epsilon_t$, so a unit shock at $t$ moves $l_{t+j-1}$ by $\alpha \sum_{k=0}^{j-1} \psi_k$ and $y_{t+j} = l_{t+j-1} + d_{t+j}$ by $r^{E}_j = \psi_j + \alpha \sum_{k=0}^{j-1} \psi_k$ for $j \ge 1$.

$\lim_{j \to \infty} r^{E}_j = \alpha \, \theta(1) / \phi(1)$: the level keeps $\alpha \psi(1)$ of every shock, and its increments $\alpha \psi(B) \epsilon_t$ are autocorrelated unless $\psi(B) = 1$, that is, unless there is no ARMA part, given that $\theta(B)$ is invertible.

Under ADAM's additive ARMA component, $y_t = l_{t-1} + a_t + \epsilon_t$ with $a_t + \epsilon_t = \psi(B) \epsilon_t$ and $l_t - l_{t-1} = \alpha \epsilon_t$, so a unit shock at $t$ moves $y_{t+j}$ by $r^{A}_j = \alpha + \psi_j$ for $j \ge 1$.
$\lim_{j \to \infty} r^{A}_j = \alpha$: the level keeps $\alpha$ of every shock, its increments $\alpha \epsilon_t$ are white noise, and the response of the ARMA part, $\psi_j$, decays to zero.

For an AR(1), $\psi_j = \phi^j$: $r^{E}_j = \phi^j + \alpha (1 - \phi^j) / (1 - \phi) \to \alpha / (1 - \phi)$, which grows without bound as $\phi \to 1$ when $\alpha > 0$, while $r^{A}_j = \alpha + \phi^j \to \alpha$.

evidence.description: Derivation of the impulse responses of a local level with an ARMA part under ARMA errors and under ADAM's additive ARMA component, and their limits.

limitations.statement: The accuracy measure of the M4 hourly tests changed after their results were seen: MASE decided the tests of C4, C5, C6 and C9 (lab run RN8), the guarantor then judged MASE unsuitable and set RMSSE (decision DC4 of the lab record), and C10 to C13 restate those hypotheses on RMSSE and test them on the same M4 test split (run RN11), so they are not independent of C4 to C6 and C9.
The t-tests and their intervals treat the series as independent; the series of one data set share calendar and weather effects, so the intervals may be too narrow.
The electricity evaluation covers one week, the 7 daily origins before 2014-09-08, of the clients of one utility; other weeks or seasons of the year may rank the methods differently.

Elapsed times depend on the machine and on the language: forecast::tbats runs in R and the other methods in Python, the M4 runs ran on a cloud machine and the electricity runs on the guarantor's computer, and each time includes its language's overhead per fit.

The lab record flags plans PL1, PL5 and PL7 with code changed after the plan; between PL1 and its run only m4_hourly.py changed, not the script the run used; between PL5 and its run only electricity_hourly.py was added; between PL7 and its run the change set the null hypothesis of superiority that PL7's design specifies.

artefacts.description: Nemenyi test on the per-series RMSSE of the six methods on the electricity data (369 series, level 0.99): mean rank of each method with its 99% interval, from run RN14 (smooth TBATS, smooth TBATS dnorm) and run RN13 (the other four).
CSV written by run RN14 with the per-method values of smooth TBATS and smooth TBATS dnorm (E5.T1), at full precision.
CSV written by run RN14 with the three t-tests of plan PL8 and the relative RMSSE and elapsed time with their intervals (E5.T3, E5.R1 to E5.R5), at full precision.
CSV written by run RN14 with the Nemenyi test of the six methods: mean ranks, intervals, critical distance (E5.T2, E5.R6 to E5.R8), at full precision.
